planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; give Milkmaid a trellis, fence, or hanging basket rim, since it trails and climbs several feet if supported.

directions: Sow seeds directly where they are to grow, since nasturtiums resent root disturbance from transplanting; keep soil on the lean side, as rich ground produces lush leaves at the expense of bloom. Milkmaid is among the palest nasturtiums grown, opening ivory-cream flowers faintly veined toward a soft yellow throat, a striking contrast to the hot oranges and reds typical of the species. Both the peppery leaves and blooms are edible and make a mild, elegant addition to salads. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage bushier growth if a fuller, less rangy plant is desired.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last spring frost in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in mild-winter zones, fall sowing gives earlier, longer bloom.

directions: Direct sow a quarter inch deep in lean, well-drained soil once it is workable; Indian Prince carries long, sturdy stems topped with semi-double, deep burnt-orange flowers backed in dusky mahogany-red, a much richer color than standard yellow or orange calendula. The long stems suit it well for cutting, and the petals have the characteristic tangy, slightly peppery flavor prized in edible-flower mixes and salads. Deadhead spent blooms every few days to keep flowers coming through the season, and expect some reliable self-sowing where it is happy.

common_name: Fiesta Gitana Calendula (Dwarf Compact Pot Marigold)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last spring frost, or a few weeks early since young plants tolerate light frost; keeps a tidy, compact shape that suits edging and containers.

directions: Direct sow shallowly in lean, well-drained soil; Fiesta Gitana stays notably dwarf and densely bushy compared with most calendula, earning it a place in edging, window boxes, and small containers where taller pot marigolds would flop. Fully double, aromatic flowers open in a cream-to-deep-orange range and stand up well above the tidy foliage mound. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom into summer, and expect the peppery-edible petals to hold their color well when sprinkled fresh over salads or baked goods.

planting.note: Start indoors 10-14 weeks before fall transplant in mild climates, or in late winter for spring bloom; rogue out any seedlings that revert toward the wild tricolor pattern to keep the strain reliably near-black.

directions: Sow indoors and cover lightly, since light aids germination; grow on cool once seedlings are up, as heat stalls this selection. Bowles' Black is named for English plantsman E. A. Bowles and produces small, velvety flowers so deeply purple-black they read as jet, each lit by a thin yellow eye and faint whisker markings. Like other Viola tricolor forms it self-sows freely once established, drifting through gravel paths and border edges, and the edible flowers make a striking dark garnish against pale dishes or frosted cakes. Some seedlings revert toward the ancestral purple-yellow-white tricolor pattern, so remove off-type plants early if a pure black planting is the goal.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes in average, well-drained soil in full sun; thin out any seedlings with plain green leaves once true leaves appear to keep the variegated strain true.

directions: Direct sow a quarter inch deep where plants are to grow, since borage resents transplanting once its taproot forms. Bill Archer is a variegated strain of common borage, its fuzzy leaves irregularly splashed with cream, while the star-shaped flowers remain the familiar brilliant blue of the species. Leaf variegation varies from plant to plant and even shifts with temperature and season, so cull any seedlings that emerge solid green to keep the planting showy. Harvest young leaves and flowers for their mild cucumber flavor, and let a few plants stand to self-sow for next year's patch.
